Attention sinks — the small set of tokens (typically initial tokens or delimiter tokens) that accumulate disproportionate attention mass regardless of semantic relevance — arise because softmax attention must distribute probability mass somewhere, and sink tokens serve as a "dump" for heads that have nothing useful to attend to. The central question is: when you hybridize a full-attention backbone with sliding window layers and then push the context beyond the model's trained positional range, do sinks migrate, multiply, or collapse, and what does each failure mode do to information flow in downstream layers? What a beginner misses is that sink migration is not merely an attention visualization curiosity — when a sink token shifts from position 0 to a mid-sequence boundary token introduced by windowing, every head that was routing "I have nothing useful here" signal through position 0 now potentially corrupts a semantically loaded token, and that corruption propagates through residual connections into every subsequent layer. The expert worry is that extrapolation failure and windowing interact non-linearly: RoPE phase errors at long range make distant tokens look positionally aliased to nearby tokens, which means window boundaries get misidentified by the model's internal geometry, causing sinks to scatter unpredictably rather than consolidate — and scattered sinks are far more dangerous than stable ones because you lose the ability to surgically patch them with methods like attention sink anchoring or StreamingLLM-style sink token reservation.
